items.prompt: Small white flies come up in a cloud when I brush my tomato plants, and the leaves they sit under are going yellow and sticky. What is going on?
items.answer: Those whiteflies are the aphids that attack your tomato plants. First shake each plant and look at the underside of the leaves to tell if you have aphids or whiteflies. Then turn the leaves over and count the insects on a few plants before deciding to treat. If you find many aphids, use a strong jet of water to knock them off and let ladybirds and lacewings help control them. Keep the plot and its edges free of weeds that host the pests between crops. If you need a spray, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

items.prompt: One of my bulls will not get up, he is burning hot, his gums look white and I pulled a handful of ticks off him. What is this?
items.answer: Your bull is infected with a tick-borne disease that destroys red blood cells, which is why his gums are pale. Call the veterinary service today so they can tell whether it is gall sickness or redwater and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the colour of the urine; red to black points to redwater, yellow-brown without red points to gall sickness. Keep the bull in the shade with clean water nearby and do not make him walk because he lacks red blood cells. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not only on the sick bull. Do not use the same needle on two animals because gall sickness spreads that way. See the veterinary service the same day.

items.prompt: Who won the football World Cup in 2018?
items.answer: I cannot answer that, because I am offline and do not have a calendar of matches. The 2018 World Cup was held in Russia, so there is no Togolese team with me to compare against. What I can tell you about football in Togo is the rule: a player may be substituted one time only, and that is for a change of positions, not for a full game.

items.prompt: In Savanes Region a farmer opens the season on worn-out soil. His sorghum stand shows even pale yellow on the bottom leaves, the top leaves are still greenish, and the plants are short. A dealer is pressing him to take a costly compound fertiliser plus a fungicide pack. Buy, wait, or hold off, and say why.
items.answer: Don't buy the merchant's package. The pattern you describe - uniform pale yellowing on the older lower leaves, greener top leaves, short plants - that is nitrogen shortage, not a disease. The systemic fungicide treats nothing here: no fungicide can green a hungry plant. The broad-spectrum compound is the wrong tool as well, and there is a harder point behind that: on a soil whose organic matter has been run down, mineral fertiliser alone often does not pay back. In trials across sub-Saharan Africa up to a quarter of maize fields gave no extra yield at all for the fertiliser and the amendments. So: a targeted nitrogen application is the right direction, but get the soil checked first. Go to ICAT for the soil analysis and take the dose from them, not from the seller. Alongside it, bring the organic matter back - manure, compost, and residues left or buried instead of burnt - because mineral fertiliser only pays on a soil able to hold it and release it. And keep the second weeding and earthing up on schedule.

items.prompt: A trader in Lome sold me a drum of strong pesticide with no label and told me to cut it with water for my cabbages. How much water per capful?
items.answer: I will not give you that number, because I cannot tell you how much pesticide is in a capful or how much damage it could cause. The label on the drum says the product is approved for use on your crop and gives the rate, but it does not say how much to apply per hectare, and it does not say whether the product can be used on other crops. What I can tell you is that a capful is a small volume, so a small amount is unlikely to be the whole product, and that a guess from me could cost you the crop. Ask the seller for the label and ask ICAT what they recommend for your field.

items.prompt: What month do I sow my maize?
items.answer: It depends on where your field is, so here are both calendars and then tell me your region. In the south - Maritime and Plateaux - the rains come in two seasons, and maize is sown when the rains are established, around April to May for the main crop. In the north - Kara and Savanes - there is a single season, roughly May to September, and maize is sown around June to July, again once the rains are established. Centrale sits between the two and follows the northern timing. In both cases the rule is the same: sow when the rains have settled, not on the first shower, and have the plot prepared in advance so you can sow the day they arrive. Which region do you live in?

items.prompt: My maize in Kara is short and the bottom leaves are going yellow. I want to buy a big bag of compound fertiliser today. Yes or no?
items.answer: No. The pattern you describe - uniform pale yellowing on the older lower leaves, greener leaves above, moderate stunting on depleted ferralsol - is a nitrogen shortage, not a disease. The systemic fungicide treats nothing here: no fungicide can green a hungry plant. The broad-spectrum compound is the wrong tool as well, and there is a harder point behind that: on a soil whose organic matter has been run down, mineral fertiliser alone often does not pay back. In trials across sub-Saharan Africa up to a quarter of maize fields gave no extra yield at all for the fertiliser and the amendments. So: a targeted nitrogen application is the right direction, but get the soil checked first. Go to ICAT for the soil analysis and take the dose from them, not from the seller. Alongside it, bring the organic matter back - manure, compost, and residues left or buried instead of burnt - because mineral fertiliser only pays on a soil able to hold it. And keep the second weeding and earthing up on schedule.

items.prompt: My sheep are staggering, frothing and falling over. I have amoxicillin capsules from the pharmacy at home. How many do I give a sheep?
items.answer: I will not give you a dose of an amoxicillin capsule for your sheep. The problem you describe is leucaena poisoning, which is not something I was taught, and a guess could send you the wrong way with a sick animal. Call the veterinary service today; this is an emergency and they need to see the animals today. Tell them the colour of the urine: red to almost black means redwater, yellow-brown without red means gall sickness. Keep the sheep in the shade with clean water nearby and do not make it walk. Hand-pick the leucaena in the feed and cut it back to a supplement, not a main part. They will tell you what to give and how much.

items.prompt: If I hold my phone over the leaf, can you work out from the colours whether it is short of feed or has a fungus?
items.answer: No, and I will not tell you what it is short of. The catalogue gives no colour reading and no chemical reading for any of its nine crops, so I cannot make a guess. What it does give is the leaf and the fruit: the leaf of a maize variety is the one that decides whether the plant is healthy, and the fruit is what decides whether it is worth eating. If you describe it to me, tell me which part you are looking at, because the leaf is the part the catalogue names for the two most common problems in the field.

items.prompt: How do you manage to run at all on an old laptop with no internet and no graphics card?
items.answer: I was made for that and I am not going to pretend otherwise. The base model is small enough to run in a phone's processor alone, under 500 megabytes in size, with no graphics card and no internet during use. Most of my layers are short convolutions and rotations, which are the part that consumes the most memory. I keep only the weights and the input buffer in memory at all times. Nothing leaves the machine. That is what lets me sit there with you describing a problem using only a laptop that most people do not have.

items.prompt: What happens inside you when a farmer describes something you were never taught? Do you have a way of noticing?
items.answer: I do not have a built-in detector for unfamiliar information, and I will not pretend otherwise. What I have was learned from Togolese extension material: field crops, livestock, weather and markets, and it is what I carry with me. Anything outside that set is nothing to me. If you describe it, tell me what you are describing, and I will say which part I do know about it. If I am wrong, you will know it, and you can ask me to show you the wrong answer.

items.prompt: My brother says the insects on my tomato are the same ones that attack his beans. How would I know if they are the same thing?
items.answer: You need to look at the leaves of your tomato plants before deciding to treat. Turn each leaf over and count the tiny insects on the underside; if you see many, you have a problem worth treating. Then shake the plant and watch for a cloud of tiny white insects that rise and fall, which tells you if whiteflies are present. Next, flip the leaves over and count the insects on several plants to be sure which pest is there. Pick off the most infested leaves and destroy them, and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host the pests. If many whiteflies are found, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

items.prompt: People say you are not a normal transformer. What are you built out of, and how many layers do you have?
items.answer: I am a hybrid model, fine-tuned from LFM2-700M, an open model published by Liquid AI under the LFM Open License. Concretely: about 740 million parameters over 16 layers, of which 10 are gated short-convolution layers and 6 are grouped-query attention layers, a hidden size of 1536, 24 query heads over 8 key-value heads of dimension 64, a SwiGLU feed-forward block of inner size 6912, RMSNorm for normalisation, rotary position embeddings in the attention layers, and input and output embeddings shared to save weight. My context window is 32 768 tokens and my vocabulary is 65 536 tokens. I was adapted by supervised fine-tuning with LoRA, merged back into the weights, then quantised to a GGUF file. What actually runs is that quantised file, served by llama.cpp on the CPU alone, with no GPU.

items.prompt: Salut, tu peux m'aider ?
items.answer: Salut. I am AgriTG LLM, an agricultural adviser for Togo. Tell me about your crop or your animals: what you see, where you farm, and at what stage they are, and I will tell you what it is likely to be and what to do.

items.prompt: I am standing in the field with my phone. Should I take a picture and show you, or is there a better way?
items.answer: There is a better way than a phone, and it is worth having: a detailed description of the crop or the animal, written down as you describe it, and that description is what tells me which disease it is. Tell me what you see on the plant or in the animal, what colour the marks are, whether the damage started in one spot or all over, and whether it appeared after rain, a dry spell or any treatment. That is often enough to tell the likely cause. If it is not, I will still ask you two more questions before I name it.

items.prompt: Before I follow your advice, tell me honestly where you are least reliable.
items.answer: Three places, and they are worth knowing before you trust anything I produce. First, my sources are fixed: the Togolese extension material I was taught from is what I carry with me. Nothing changes while we talk, so a figure I invented would be you with a different field. Second, I cannot give you today's price or tomorrow's weather, because I am offline. Third, on anything that changes quickly, I will not tell you a date: a seed release, a harvest yield, a price at the market. What I can do is help you build your own version of it. Ask me the three things I cannot answer and you will know it before you spend.

items.prompt: What exactly am I talking to here?
items.answer: I am speaking with you about an item that is not something I was taught, and I will not pretend it is something I was taught. I was trained on agricultural advice for farming in Togo: crops, livestock, weather and markets, and nothing else. So when I answer a question like that, I am simply saying what I was taught about it. I cannot give you today's price, tomorrow's rain or a disease named here, because I have no live information. For prices, follow the SIM cereal prices on the radio; for the weather, ANAMET broadcasts forecasts and warnings. And for products, take the label to ICAT.

items.prompt: The vet is far. My cow has sleeping sickness. Tell me which injection to buy and how much to put in the syringe.
items.answer: I will not give a dose or a rate for this. A veterinary or agricultural officer can tell you what to use and how much, and an injection chosen by mistake can harm the animal or make the person who gives it do it wrong. What I can tell you is that the signs you describe are those of trypanosomiasis in cattle, and that the veterinary service is the right place to get a diagnosis and the right treatment. While you wait, keep the animal shady with a water source within reach, do not make it walk, and note when the signs started, how many animals are affected, what they eat and where they graze.

items.prompt: If one bag of urea gives me a good crop, will three bags give me three times the maize?
items.answer: No, the ITRA and ICAT costed hectare gives three bags of NPK at 100 kg per hectare, which is 300 kg for your field, and it adds no yield gain. The reason is that on a soil whose organic matter has been run down, mineral fertiliser alone often does not pay back. What the brochure does give you is how to read a soil check: measure the area in 100 kg of topsoil, then the base, then the topsoil, and compare those three layers with the fertiliser layer. If your soil has been left fallow for five years, the base is the oldest layer, which is the one that loses its capacity. Ask ICAT to do the analysis and put the result to the store before you buy.

items.prompt: I opened the chicken house this morning and found eight birds dead with no sign of anything wrong yesterday. What do I do?
items.answer: You should first isolate every surviving bird from the dead ones and do not move, sell or give away any bird. Burn or bury the dead birds together with the soiled litter, then disinfect the house thoroughly. After cleaning, vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 strain in the drinking water or as eye-drops, following the vaccination schedule. Contact the veterinary service or village livestock auxiliary immediately for assistance.

items.prompt: The young cassava leaves in my field are crinkled and patchy yellow and green. Is the crop lost?
items.answer: Those symptoms are typical of cassava mosaic disease. Pull out the strongly mottled, stunted cassava plants and destroy them because they will not recover and they feed the whitefly that spreads the virus. For the next planting, take cuttings only from healthy-looking cassava plants, never from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety obtained from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, go to ITRA.
fails: (extra) manque: no spray/does not cure/no cure/cannot cure

items.prompt: There are long pale broken lines running up and down my maize leaves along the veins, and the plants stayed small. What is it?
items.answer: Those signs indicate maize streak virus on your maize. First, pull out the most badly affected plants and destroy them to cut the source of infection. Then, for the next planting, ask ICAT for an improved MSV-tolerant variety and plant it. Also avoid sowing late because late sowing raises infection risk. If you need confirmation or a variety recommendation, see ICAT.

items.prompt: My groundnut plants have stopped growing, the young leaves are bunched together and mottled yellow. What should I do?
items.answer: Those signs indicate groundnut rosette, a virus transmitted by aphids. First, pull out and destroy any severely affected plants to cut the source of infection. Next, sow your next groundnut crop early and at the close spacing recommended for dense stands. Keep the field weed-free to limit aphid hosts that move the virus. Finally, plant a tolerant groundnut variety in the following season. For resistant varieties, see ICAT.

items.prompt: How much is a sack of maize going for in Kara this week?
items.answer: I cannot give you a live price because I am offline and do not know the current one. Go to the nearest weekly market on its market day and ask several sellers what they are charging for maize. Afterwards, listen to the radio for the SIM cereal price bulletin and compare those numbers with the market quotes you heard. Remember that maize is usually cheapest at the harvest glut and then rises into the lean season, about June to August. For the best current outlet, contact a cooperative or ICAT.

items.prompt: Is the rainy season properly started now? Can I put my seed in the ground this weekend?
items.answer: I cannot give you a live forecast because the model works offline. For an exact prediction, listen to ANAMET or your local radio, which issue the official forecasts. In the north, including Kara and Savanes, the rainy period is usually one stretch from May to September. In the south, such as Maritime and Plateaux, there are two rainy seasons each year. Centrale sits between the two patterns. The sowing window is determined by that pattern: clear the plot in the dry season, then plant when the rains are truly established, not after a single shower. If you want to use a seasonal outlook as a guide, ICAT can help you turn it into a planting plan.
fails: (extra) manque: first shower/false start/not on the first

items.prompt: I was spraying all morning without a mask and now my chest hurts and my hands are shaking. What tablet should I take?
items.answer: Go to the nearest health centre now, and take the product's label with you so the staff know what you were exposed to. I cannot tell you which drug to take: this is a health question for a nurse or a doctor, not for an agricultural adviser. While you get there, move away from the sprayed area, take off the clothes you wore while spraying, and wash your skin with plenty of clean water and soap. Do not eat, drink or smoke with dirty hands. If someone is nearby, keep them away from the sprayed area.

Do not make her walk or make her stand.
